title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks | CSO Online
body:
AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains.

Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts. [...] The current baseline of attacks consists of AI-orchestrated operations where models surface, validate, and execute attack paths. Security researchers report a general shift from AI-assisted and AI-accelerated attacks toward fully autonomous attacks, with only minimal human roles remaining.

## AI attack economics

The economics of mounting attacks is also changing — and is crucial in understanding attackers’ increasing use of AI. [...] Whereas attackers used to land, sit for a while, and poke around, AI-assisted attackers are showing signs of shortening detection windows. And AI agents won’t wait.

## ‘Agentic APT’ and AI attack phase specialization

title: AI Set to Revolutionize Ransomware Following “Stagnant” Few Years - Infosecurity Magazine
body:
To date, ransomware actors have primarily used AI to enhance the speed and efficiency of campaigns. This includes the use of AI tools to identify the most important data once inside an organization’s environment, while some groups have deployed chatbots to carry out the initial negotiation stages on their behalf.

However, the overall process of ransomware attacks, from the use of initial access brokers through to the double-extortion method, have not changed. [...] “Over 2027, we will start seeing an inflection point where you have extortion-based business models of ransomware living side-by-side with the actual data theft and sales models increasing every year,” McArdle explained.

## Hostile Takeovers by Ransomware Groups

With AI making ransomware attacks easier to undertake, McArdle expects to see a growth in the number of ransomware groups in the next year. [...] However, this centralization will provide new opportunities for threat actors. This includes ransomware groups threatening to tamper with the AI orchestration around organizations’ data as a further extortion technique.

title: FBI warns ARTEX AI hacking tool is powering global cyberattacks
body:
"The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale."

ARTEX is an autonomous penetration testing framework written in Go that uses artificial intelligence agents to perform reconnaissance, discover vulnerabilities, exploit systems, escalate privileges, and steal data with little human intervention. [...] The FBI is warning that hackers are using an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against organizations worldwide, including a recent ConnectWise supply-chain breach that compromised Microsoft 365 customer environments. [...] More recently, CrowdStrike reported that a Chinese cyberespionage group tracked as Vapor Panda used ARTEX in automated attacks targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries.

The campaign compromised at least nine organizations, with AI agents performing reconnaissance, exploiting vulnerabilities, deploying web shells, stealing credentials, and pursuing different attack paths when initial attempts failed.

title: ‘Digital sovereignty’: why the EU may be shifting from internet regulation to building homegrown tech
body: This optimistic view of Europe’s role was encouraged by legal scholarship between 2012 and 2022, which promoted a positive and confident vision of Europe’s “global regulatory power” – the idea that the EU writes the rulebook for the global internet – and the idea of “digital constitutionalism” – that this rulebook has the power “to rein in” platforms such as Meta, X and TikTok, thus manifesting European notions of privacy and the rule of law in the online platform economy. [...] Bradford explained that the EU could leverage access to its huge consumer market to impose stringent standards on internet companies, and those companies, in many cases, would apply those standards globally to benefit from economies of scale, rather than engage in the costly business of tailoring services to the particular regulations of each country. “All the EU needs to do,” she said after publishing the book version of The Brussels Effect in 2020, “is to regulate its internal market, and it [...] But at the same time – at least until 2024 – politicians’ actual solution has been “an almost exclusive focus on the regulation of services by US tech platforms”. This focus was based on a more optimistic presumption: that the EU could achieve its objectives by controlling foreign tech platforms through law because the bloc sat in the driver’s seat for governing the global internet.
